scope_allowed: Relevance of the validation activities to the COU

models.name: Model A: Explicit-thread Screw in Cortico-cancellous Vertebral Segment
models.what_it_computes: Nonlinear force–displacement response during axial extraction, thread flank contact pressure distribution, local bone plastic strain and damage indices, and predicted initiation of pullout.

models.name: Model B: Axisymmetric Unit-Cell Interface with Anisotropic Bone Surrogate
models.what_it_computes: Effective interface shear capacity, initial purchase stiffness (pre-yield slope), insertion-torque proxy from frictional seating work, and progressive loss of engagement under small-amplitude cyclic loading.

mechanisms.name: Monotonic axial pullout
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Determines the maximum resistance to extraction during adverse loading and provides a benchmark for primary fixation strength.

mechanisms.name: Immediate post-insertion purchase
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Captures primary stability at time zero, informing likelihood of micromotion before fusion and correlation with insertion torque.

mechanisms.name: Low-amplitude cyclic toggling
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Assesses early loosening pathways from physiologic micromotion that degrade thread engagement without catastrophic failure.

mechanisms.name: Transverse pedicle wall strip-out
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Evaluates off-axis load transfer and risk of pedicle wall compromise that can precipitate loss of fixation.

deviation.detail: All credibility factors are scored on a 0–12 confidence index (0, 4, 8, 12) with rationales recorded per model-by-mechanism cell.

spans: For axial pullout, Model A predicts peak extraction force within 7% of experiment (1640 N vs 1760 ± 310 N), with early stiffness within 9% (2.5 vs 2.7 ± 0.5 kN/mm).
For monotonic axial pullout, Model A’s peak force estimate of 1640 N fell below the experimental mean of 1760 N by 6.8%, within the predefined 10% tolerance for central tendency.
The early stiffness up to 0.5 mm was 2.5 kN/mm versus 2.7 kN/mm measured, a 9% difference.
findings.span: For axial pullout, Model A predicts peak extraction force within 7% of experiment (1640 N vs 1760 ± 310 N), with early stiffness within 9% (2.5 vs 2.7 ± 0.5 kN/mm).

spans: Monotonic axial pullout followed an ASTM F543-like protocol.
Tests were performed in 37 °C Ringer’s solution at 5 mm/min crosshead speed.

Axial pullout was conducted at 37 °C in Ringer’s solution at 5 mm/min; instrument fixtures and clamps were represented in the models by displacement constraints on vertebral boundary surfaces and stabilization near the pedicle entrance.
findings.span: Monotonic axial pullout followed an ASTM F543-like protocol.

spans: For immediate engagement, Model A’s seating-work-derived torque proxy matches within 5% of measured torque (1.05 vs 1.10 ± 0.30 N·m).

For immediate engagement, Model A’s computation of frictional seating work integrated over the engaged interface produced a torque proxy of 1.05 N·m against the instrumented 6 edicle screw FEA driver’s 1.10 N·m mean, a 5% difference.
The pre-yield axial stiffness immediately after seating was predicted as 2.9 kN/mm compared with 3.0 kN/mm measured.
findings.span: For immediate engagement, Model A’s seating-work-derived torque proxy matches within 5% of measured torque (1.05 vs 1.10 ± 0.30 N·m).

spans: Immediate engagement was characterized by two mea-surements First, insertion torque was recorded using an instrumented driver during the final two turns of seating; the mean torque was 1.10 N·m (SD 0.30, n = 14 cadaveric vertebrae) with foam-block corroboration used only for independent verification of the driver system (n = 8 blocks, 15 pcf nominal density).
Second, post-seating axial stiffness was measured from small-amplitude load–displacement cycles; the pre-yield slope averaged 3.0 kN/mm (SD 0.6).
findings.span: Immediate engagement was characterized by two mea-surements First, insertion torque was recorded using an instrumented driver during the final two turns of seating; the mean torque was 1.10 N·m (SD 0.30, n = 14 cadaveric vertebrae) with foam-block corroboration used only for independent verification of the driver system (n = 8 blocks, 15 pcf nominal density).

spans: The head of the screw is driven by imposed displacement for extraction or by rotation plus axial force for seating simulations; the vertebral segment is constrained at boundary faces representing the anterior and lateral cortices, and a zone around the pedicle entrance is stabilized to mimic fixture constraints.

spans: The thread–bone friction coefficient was sampled from a normal distribution N(0.24, 0.05) in sensitivity runs; the nominal value 0.24 was used for the primary predictions reported.

The seating-work torque proxy in both models was computed by integrating tangential traction times circumferential sliding distance over the engaged interface and dividing by the instantaneous rotation rate; this proxy was compared to measured insertion torque to assess whether sliding friction dominated seating resistance.
findings.span: The thread–bone friction coefficient was sampled from a normal distribution N(0.24, 0.05) in sensitivity runs; the nominal value 0.24 was used for the primary predictions reported.

spans: Under small-amplitude toggling, Model A reaches a 20% stiffness reduction at 5300 cycles versus 6000 ± 1500 cycles measured.

Under low-amplitude cyclic toggling, Model A’s continuum damage with kinematic effect yielded a 20% reduction in axial stiffness at 5300 cycles, versus a measured mean of 6000 cycles and SD of 1500 cycles.

spans: Low-amplitude cyclic toggling is intended to represent physi-ologic micromotion under small lateral excursions, implemented here as sinusoidal lateral displacement of ±0.3 mm at 2 Hz under a constant compressive bias of 150 N.

spans: In transverse loading, Model A underpredicts failure by 27% (380 vs 520 ± 160 N).
For transverse pedicle wall strip-out, Model A’s lateral head load applied at 1 mm/min produced a failure force of 380 N on average, 27% lower than the experimental mean of 520 N (SD 160).
findings.span: In transverse loading, Model A underpredicts failure by 27% (380 vs 520 ± 160 N).

spans: Failure initiated as tensile cracking in the pedicle wall at locations coincident with high tensile strains in the model, but the absence of an explicit crack-propagation formulation and a relatively coarse cortical mesh limit confidence in the quantitative prediction.
findings.span: Failure initiated as tensile cracking in the pedicle wall at locations coincident with high tensile strains in the model, but the absence of an explicit crack-propagation formulation and a relatively coarse cortical mesh limit confidence in the quantitative prediction.

spans: Transverse pedicle wall strip-out tests applied lateral force perpendicular to the screw axis at 1 mm/min until failure, defined by a sharp drop in load accompanied by pedicle wall cracking.

In transverse strip-out, lateral head load was applied at 1 mm/min until pedicle wall failure; the model boundary conditions captured the clamp constraints but, due to geometric variabilities, did not reproduce wall notch sharpness at the microscale.
findings.span: Transverse pedicle wall strip-out tests applied lateral force perpendicular to the screw axis at 1 mm/min until failure, defined by a sharp drop in load accompanied by pedicle wall cracking.

spans: The mean failure force for six pedicles was 520 N (SD 160), with failures initiating as tensile cracking at the pedicle wall near the notch created by the thread path.
findings.span: The mean failure force for six pedicles was 520 N (SD 160), with failures initiating as tensile cracking at the pedicle wall near the notch created by the thread path.

spans: Transverse pedicle wall strip-out interrogates off-axis load transfer when a lateral force is applied perpendicular to the screw axis, causing tensile stress in the pedicle wall and potential wall compromise.
Transverse wall strip-out represents an adverse-event pathway outside the primary fixation metrics but relevant for safety margins.
findings.span: Transverse pedicle wall strip-out interrogates off-axis load transfer when a lateral force is applied perpendicular to the screw axis, causing tensile stress in the pedicle wall and potential wall compromise.

spans: Model B is an axisymmetric unit-cell representation focusing on the local mechanics of thread flank engagement with cancellous bone.

To scale unit-cell results to full-screw predictions for monotonic pullout, the model multiplies per-thread force by the number of engaged turns estimated from thread depth and purchase length; this scaling is only used for sensitivity analysis and is not intended to replace Model A for full-segment predictions.
findings.span: Model B is an axisymmetric unit-cell representation focusing on the local mechanics of thread flank engagement with cancellous bone.
